result: AMH is expressed in migratory GnRH neurons during embryonic development in both mouse and human fetuses. In mice, Amh expression is detected at E12.5 in FACS-isolated GnRH neurons and increases from E12.5 to adult life (PN90). In human fetuses at GW11, AMH is expressed in GnRH neurons but not on vomeronasal/terminal nerves, and GnRH neurons are the only AMH-expressing neurons in the forebrain at this stage.
evaluation: Claims C4, C33-C37 are well-supported by multiple experimental approaches including FACS isolation with RT-PCR (Figure 1a,b), immunofluorescence in nasal explants (Figure 1d-f), and immunofluorescence in human fetal sections (Figure 1h-o). The data demonstrate AMH expression in migratory GnRH neurons across species and developmental stages with appropriate controls and replication (n=2 human fetuses, multiple mouse samples).

result: AMH functions as a pro-motility factor for GnRH neurons through the Amhr2/Bmpr1b receptor complex and MAPK pathway activation. AMH treatment increases ERK1/2 phosphorylation in GN11 cells in a dose- and time-dependent manner, and significantly increases GN11 cell motility at doses of 50-250 ng/ml. This effect is prevented by MAPK inhibition (U0126), AMHR2 neutralizing antibody, and siRNA knockdown of Amhr2 or Bmpr1b.
evaluation: Claims C5, C58-C66, and C84 are strongly supported by convergent evidence from Western blot analysis (Figure 5b,c), transwell migration assays (Figure 5d,e), and receptor knockdown experiments (Figure 5f,g). The mechanistic pathway is well-established through pharmacological inhibition and genetic knockdown with appropriate controls. Statistical analyses are properly conducted with sufficient replication (n=3-13 depending on experiment).

result: Pharmacological or genetic invalidation of Amhr2 disrupts GnRH neuronal migration and olfactory/vomeronasal system development. In utero injection of Amhr2 neutralizing antibody at E12.5 causes accumulation of GnRH cells in the nasal compartment and decreased numbers in the ventral forebrain by E14.5, without affecting cell survival. Amhr2-/- embryos at E13.5 show incomplete olfactory bulb innervation and GnRH neurons clustered in the nasal compartment with fewer reaching the ventral forebrain.
evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C28-C29, and C38-C42 are well-supported by in vivo experiments using both pharmacological (in utero injection, Figure 2) and genetic (Amhr2-/- mice, Figure 3) approaches. The iDISCO/light sheet microscopy provides comprehensive 3D visualization (n=2 per genotype). Cell counting shows altered distribution without affecting survival (Figure 2g,h), supporting a migration rather than survival defect. The convergence of two independent experimental approaches strengthens the conclusions.

result: Adult Amhr2-deficient mice exhibit reduced GnRH neuron numbers, impaired reproductive hormone secretion, and decreased fertility in a gene dose-dependent manner. Amhr2-/- mice show a 40% reduction in GnRH cell number in both sexes, reduced LH levels and pulse frequency, fewer corpora lutea, and severely impaired fertility. Amhr2+/- females display an intermediate phenotype with reduced LH levels, pulse frequency, and fertility, while Amhr2+/- males show only reduced litter frequency. Amhr2-/- males are completely infertile due to persistent Müllerian duct syndrome.
evaluation: Claims C8, C30-C31, C43-C51, C89, and C92 are comprehensively supported by multiple physiological measurements in adult mice (Figure 4). GnRH cell counting (n=7 per group), LH measurements (n=3-5), ovarian histology (n=4-5), LH pulsatility (n=3-5), and fertility tests (n=3-12) all show consistent gene dose-dependent effects. Statistical analyses are appropriate with one-way ANOVA and post-hoc tests. The intermediate phenotype in heterozygotes is particularly well-documented across multiple parameters.

result: Loss-of-function heterozygous mutations in AMH and AMHR2 were identified in 3% (4/136) of CHH probands through whole-exome sequencing. Three probands harbor missense mutations in AMH (p.Thr99Ser, p.Pro151Ser, p.Asp238Glu) in the N-terminal pro-protein domain affecting highly conserved amino acids. One female proband harbors an in-frame 27-nucleotide deletion in AMHR2 (p.Gly445_Leu453del) within the catalytic intracellular serine/threonine kinase domain.
evaluation: Claims C3, C32, C67-C71, and C101 are supported by whole-exome sequencing data from a well-characterized CHH cohort (136 probands without mutations in known CHH genes). The mutations are documented in Table 1 and Figure 6 with appropriate genomic and protein-level annotations. Conservation analysis (Figure 6c,f) supports functional importance. However, the small number of identified mutations (n=4) limits statistical power for prevalence estimates, though the 3% rate is consistent with other rare CHH genes.

result: AMH mutations identified in CHH patients are loss-of-function, showing significantly reduced AMH secretion and impaired GnRH neuron migration and hormone secretion in vitro. All three AMH mutants (p.Pro151Ser, p.Asp238Glu, p.Thr99Ser) show reduced AMH secretion in COS-7 cells and prevent AMH-dependent GN11 cell migration. The p.Thr99Ser mutation additionally reduces GnRH secretion in GT1-7 cells.
evaluation: Claims C72-C75, C95, C97-C98 are well-supported by functional validation experiments (Figure 7a-c, Table 1). AMH secretion assays (n=3), transwell migration assays (n=11-30 depending on condition), and GnRH secretion assays (n=3) all demonstrate loss-of-function effects. The experiments appropriately use wild-type AMH as positive control and mock transfection as negative control. Statistical analyses with one-way ANOVA and post-hoc tests are appropriate.

result: The AMHR2 p.Gly445_Leu453del mutation identified in a CHH patient is loss-of-function, significantly impairing AMH-induced GN11 cell migration and GnRH secretion in GT1-7 cells. AMH treatment increases migration and GnRH secretion in cells expressing wild-type AMHR2, but these effects are significantly reduced with the mutant receptor.
evaluation: Claims C76-C79 and C100 are supported by functional validation experiments (Figure 7d,e). Transwell migration assays (n=10-12) and GnRH secretion assays (n=3) demonstrate loss-of-function effects of the AMHR2 deletion. Two-way ANOVA with appropriate post-hoc tests shows significant interaction between genotype and AMH treatment. The experiments include proper controls (SFM vs AMH treatment, WT vs mutant).

result: Computational modeling suggests the AMHR2 p.Gly445_Leu453del deletion may result in alterations in intracellular signaling through changes in protein dynamics, particularly in the activation loop region, despite maintaining overall protein fold.
evaluation: Claim C80 is based on computational modeling (Figure 7f-i, Figure 7—figure supplements 1-2) showing differences in RMSF between wild-type and mutant AMHR2. While the modeling is technically sound (100 ns MD simulations in triplicate for mutant), the functional significance of the observed dynamic differences is speculative. The modeling supports but does not definitively prove altered signaling, and the claim is appropriately hedged with 'may result' and 'it is possible.'

result: GN11 and GT1-7 immortalized GnRH cell lines express Amh, Amhr2, and type I receptors (Acvr1, Bmpr1a), with GT1-7 cells showing higher expression levels. Notably, only GN11 cells (migratory) express Bmpr1b, suggesting Amhr2/Bmpr1b signaling may be a hallmark of migratory GnRH neurons.
evaluation: Claims C53-C56 are supported by quantitative RT-PCR data (Figure 5a, n=3-4). Statistical comparisons with unpaired t-tests show significant differences in expression levels between cell lines. Claim C57 is an inference based on differential Bmpr1b expression, which is reasonable given that GN11 represents migratory and GT1-7 represents post-migratory GnRH neurons, though this interpretation is appropriately hedged as 'may be.'

result: Mono-allelic Amhr2 inactivation in mice does not significantly alter GnRH neuronal migration (normal GnRH cell numbers in adults) but is sufficient to impair LH secretion, LH pulsatility, and fertility in females. In males, only litter frequency is reduced, suggesting altered sexual behavior rather than fecundity.
evaluation: Claims C86-C88 are supported by data in Figure 4i-n showing no difference in GnRH cell number between Amhr2+/+ and Amhr2+/- mice (n=7), but significant differences in LH levels (n=4-5), LH pulse frequency (n=4-5), and fertility parameters (n=3-12). The inference about male sexual behavior (C88) is reasonable based on the selective reduction in litter frequency without affecting pups per litter, though this interpretation is appropriately presented as speculation ('suggesting').

result: The GnRH migratory defect in Amhr2-deficient embryos is independent of genetic sex, and Amh/Amhr2 signaling may regulate GnRH migration during embryonic development and GnRH/LH secretion postnatally.
evaluation: Claim C90 is supported by data showing similar GnRH cell loss in both male and female Amhr2-/- mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, n=3 males, n=7 females). Claim C91 is speculation based on the temporal pattern of phenotypes (embryonic migration defects vs. postnatal secretion defects), which is reasonable given the data but appropriately presented as speculation ('we speculate').

result: Part of the reproductive phenotype of Amhr2-/- mice is likely due to lack of ovarian Amh, though AMH directly increases GnRH and LH secretion, supporting a role in neuroendocrine regulation of fertility.
evaluation: Claim C93 is an inference based on established knowledge about ovarian Amh function (supported by citations to Vigier et al., 1984; Durlinger et al., 2001, 1999) and is appropriately hedged as 'likely.' Claim C94 is supported by current experimental data (Figures 5, 7) and previous work (Cimino et al., 2016). The authors appropriately acknowledge that dissecting specific contributions would require tissue-specific knockouts.

result: The decreased AMH secretion of mutants might result from altered protein trafficking leading to ER accumulation, and AMH mutants may cause dominant negative effects by forming heterodimers with wild-type AMH.
evaluation: Claims C96 and C99 are speculative mechanistic explanations for the observed loss-of-function effects. While the speculation is reasonable and supported by knowledge of proAMH cleavage sites (Mamsen et al., 2015; Pankhurst and McLennan, 2013), no direct experimental evidence for ER accumulation or heterodimer formation is provided. These are appropriately presented as speculation ('might result,' 'it is plausible') but remain unvalidated hypotheses.

result: The 3% mutational prevalence of AMH/AMHR2 in CHH is consistent with the genetic landscape where most CHH genes have low prevalence (<5%). Variable expressivity was observed in families carrying the same mutation, consistent with CHH representing the severe end of a spectrum, likely involving digenic/oligogenic inheritance, epigenetic regulation, or non-genetic factors.
evaluation: Claim C102 is supported by comparison to established CHH genetics (Boehm et al., 2015). Claim C103 is supported by pedigree data (Figure 6b,e) showing variable phenotypes in family members with the same mutation. Claim C104 is based on established knowledge about CHH genetics (supported by citations to Boehm et al., 2015; Sykiotis et al., 2010; Pitteloud et al., 2007). However, the small number of families (n=4) limits the strength of conclusions about variable expressivity.

result: AMH and AMHR2 have pleiotropic roles in both Müllerian duct regression and GnRH neuron migration. Homozygous/compound heterozygous mutations cause PMDS in males, while monoallelic defects do not cause PMDS but can contribute to CHH. Two mutations identified in the CHH cohort (AMH p.Pro151Ser, AMHR2 p.Gly445_Leu453del) were previously associated with recessive PMDS. Different mechanistic actions and tissue-specific signaling may guide the final phenotype.
evaluation: Claims C105-C110 are supported by established knowledge (citations to Imbeaud et al., 1995; Mishina et al., 1996; Josso and Clemente, 2003; Picard et al., 2017; Josso et al., 2005) and clinical data from CHH patients showing no PMDS with heterozygous mutations. Claim C111 is speculation about mechanisms, which is reasonable but unvalidated. The pleiotropic role conclusion (C110) is well-supported by the convergence of genetic and functional data.

result: AMH/AMHR2 mutations affecting GnRH cell motility were found in both KS and nCHH individuals, suggesting GnRH migratory defects could occur in some nCHH cases. This challenges the dogma that migration defects cause only KS, not nCHH. Evidence suggests CHH genes segregate into three categories (KS only, nCHH only, or both), and some nCHH cases might result from defective vomeronasal/terminal nerve projections affecting GnRH migration.
evaluation: Claims C112-C116 are supported by patient data (Table 1) and functional validation (Figure 7) showing migration defects in both KS and nCHH patients. Claims C119-C120 are inferences based on current findings and cited evidence (Casoni et al., 2016; Taroc et al., 2017; Boehm et al., 2015) about the role of vomeronasal/terminal nerves. The challenge to existing dogma (C114) is appropriately supported, though the speculation about nCHH mechanisms (C120) requires further validation.

result: Amh signaling contributes to the correct development of the ventral branch of the vomeronasal/terminal nerves in the brain through a paracrine mechanism, based on Amh expression only in GnRH neurons and Amhr2 expression on the axonal scaffold.
evaluation: Claim C85 is a hypothesis based on expression patterns (Figure 1) and phenotypes in Amhr2-deficient mice (Figures 2-3). While the expression data support the possibility of paracrine signaling, direct evidence for this mechanism (e.g., conditional knockouts, rescue experiments) is not provided. The hypothesis is reasonable and appropriately presented as such ('we hypothesize'), but remains speculative.

result: Background knowledge claims about CHH, GnRH physiology, AMH signaling, and the role of vomeronasal/terminal nerves in GnRH migration.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C10-C27, C81-C83, C117-C118 represent established scientific knowledge supported by appropriate citations throughout the manuscript. These provide necessary context for interpreting the novel findings. The citations are to peer-reviewed publications and the claims are consistent with current understanding in the field.
